'''Carlos Castillo-Chavez''' (born March 29, 1952) is a Mexican-American [[mathematician]]. He held positions as a [[Distinguished professor|Regents Professor]] and the [[Joaquín Bustoz, Jr.|Joaquín Bustoz Jr.]] Professor of [[Mathematical Biology]] at [[Arizona State University]].<ref name="titleAwards/Honors">{{cite web |title=CCC ASU |url=https://sols.asu.edu/carlos-castillo-chavez |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022120527/https://sols.asu.edu/carlos-castillo-chavez |archive-date=2019-10-22 |access-date=2008-03-02}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=mtbi.asu.edu |url=http://mtbi.asu.edu/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022120537/https://mtbi.asu.edu/ |archive-date=2019-10-22 |access-date=2008-02-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Mathematical and Statistical Approaches to AIDS Epidemiology |series=Lecture Notes in Biomathematics |date=1989 |editor-last=Castillo-Chavez |editor-first=Carlos |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-642-93454-4  |volume=83 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-93454-4 |isbn=978-3-540-52174-7 |issn=0341-633X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Castillo-Chavez founded the Mathematical and Theoretical Biology Institute (MTBI) at [[Cornell University]] in 1996. His research and publications focus on mathematics, social structures, and epidemiology.

==Biography==
Carlos Castillo-Chavez was born on March 29, 1952, in [[Mexico]], immigrating to the [[United States]] in 1974, at age 22. He worked in a cheese factory in [[Wisconsin]] before continuing his studies. He attended the [[University of Wisconsin–Stevens Point]], graduating in 1976 with degrees in mathematics and Spanish literature.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Science Education {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |url=https://www.aaas.org/focus-areas/science-education |access-date=2023-03-05 |website=www.aaas.org}}</ref> He earned a [[Master of Science|MS]] in Mathematics from the [[University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newswise.com/articles/asu-professor-is-appointed-to-committee-on-the-national-medal-of-science-by-president-obama |title=ASU Professor Is Appointed to Committee on the National Medal of Science by President Obama |access-date=2013-05-11 }}</ref> He earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 1984. Before joining [[Arizona State University]] in 2004, he was a professor at [[Cornell University]] for 18 years. He has published scientific articles and books, and served on committees for organizations such as the [[National Science Foundation]], the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], the [[National Institutes of Health]], the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]], and the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="titleCarlos Castillo-Chavez">{{cite web|url=http://math.asu.edu/~chavez/|title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez, Regents and Joaquin Bustoz Jr. Professor (of Mathematics)|access-date=2008-03-02|archive-date=2008-05-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516202651/http://math.asu.edu/%7Echavez}}</ref> From 2016 to 2018, he served as [[Rector (academia)|rector]] of [[Yachay University|Yachay Tech University]] in [[Ecuador]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Castillo-Chavez |first1=Carlos |title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez |url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/carlos-castillo-chavez/ |website=LinkedIn |publisher=LinkedIn Corporation |access-date=16 February 2024}}</ref><ref name="cmdit">{{cite web |title=Dr. Carlos Castillo-Chavez - CMD-IT/ACM Richard Tapia Conference |url=https://tapiaconference.cmd-it.org/about/richard-tapia-award/dr-carlos-castillo-chavez/ |website=CMDiT |publisher=Center for Minorities and People with Disabilities in IT |access-date=16 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200924103329/https://tapiaconference.cmd-it.org/about/richard-tapia-award/dr-carlos-castillo-chavez/ |archive-date=24 September 2020}}</ref>

A In 2006, [[Arizona State University]] described him as an expert in [[Mathematical modelling of infectious disease|epidemiological modeling]], and a contributor to the literature on the progression of diseases.<ref>[http://www.asu.edu/news/stories/200603/20060323_regents_chavez.htm asu.edu], Regents' Professor: Carlos Castillo-Chavez</ref>
[[File:Ronald Mickens and Carlos Castillo-Chavez at a banquet.jpg|alt=Carlos Castillo-Chavez (right) and physicist Ronald E. Mickens stand at a banquet during the 2012 Ford Fellows Conference|thumb|Carlos Castillo-Chavez (right) and physicist [[Ronald E. Mickens]] at a banquet during the 2012 Ford Fellows Conference]]
According to a September 2020 update, his 52 PhD students included 21 women, 29 from U.S. underrepresented groups, and 7 from [[Latin America]].<ref name="cmdit"></ref> He also mentored over 500 undergraduates, primarily through the Mathematical and Theoretical Biology Institute.<ref>{{cite web | title=Thinking Out Loud &#124; Brown University | url=https://www.brown.edu/campus-life/events/thinking-out-loud/carlos-castillo-chavez }}</ref> He has been recognized for work aimed at enhancing academic success, and for providing research opportunities for underrepresented groups in mathematics and biology.<ref>[http://www.aaas.org/aboutaaas/awards/mentor/mentor2007.shtml AAAS Mentor Award] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130823091738/http://www.aaas.org/aboutaaas/awards/mentor/mentor2007.shtml |date=2013-08-23 }} announcement</ref> According to the [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]], Castillo-Chavez is listed as one of the top doctoral advisors in mathematics, and is noted as the only Latino mathematician in their top 250 list.<ref>{{cite web | title=Extrema - the Mathematics Genealogy Project | url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/extrema.php }}</ref>

In 2020, he retired from Arizona State University after resigning from his posts the previous year. An ASU investigation substantiated a graduate student report that he created a hostile environment and engaged in harassment, but the matter was closed without further action upon his retirement. According to reporting on the investigation, his "tough love" approach was cited by both supporters and detractors as a source of support and conflict, respectively.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mervis |first1=J |last2=Stellino |first2=M |title=Acclaimed mentor of minority mathematicians relied on tough love—but some say he went too far |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/acclaimed-mentor-minority-mathematicians-relied-tough-love-some-say-he-went-too-far |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240216190449/https://www.science.org/content/article/acclaimed-mentor-minority-mathematicians-relied-tough-love-some-say-he-went-too-far |archive-date=16 February 2024 |access-date=16 February 2024 |website=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)}}</ref>

Castillo-Chavez founded the Applied Mathematics in the Life and Social Sciences BS and PhD programs (2008) at the [[Simon A. Levin]] Mathematical, Computational, and Modeling Sciences Center at [[Arizona State University]].<ref>http://shesc.asu.edu/graduate/phd-program/applied-mathematics-life-and-social-sciences {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160327073321/http://shesc.asu.edu/graduate/phd-program/applied-mathematics-life-and-social-sciences |date=2016-03-27 }} 11 December 2017</ref><ref>https://shesc.asu.edu/undergraduate/bs-applied-mathematics-life-and-social-sciences {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304015319/http://shesc.asu.edu/undergraduate/bs-applied-mathematics-life-and-social-sciences |date=2016-03-04 }} 16 August 2019</ref>

Castillo-Chavez established the Mathematical and Theoretical Biology Institute (MTBI) at Cornell University in 1996. It moved to Arizona State University in the spring of 2004.<ref name="nsf-mtbi">{{cite web |title=Award Abstract #1101872: The Mathematical and Theoretical Biology Institute (MTBI) |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1101872 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240216232536/https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1101872 |archive-date=16 February 2024 |access-date=16 February 2024 |website=www.nsf.gov |publisher=National Science Foundation}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=QRLSSP {{!}} Simon A. Levin Mathematical, Computational and Modeling Sciences Center |url=https://mcmsc.asu.edu/institutes/qrlssp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231206171911/https://mcmsc.asu.edu/qrlssp/about/about-us |archive-date=6 December 2023 |website=mcmsc.asu.edu}}</ref> From 1996 to 2004, MTBI received funding from Cornell University and [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] (T-Division). The [[National Science Foundation]], the [[National Security Agency]], and Arizona State University have also provided partial funding. As of 2021-2022, it was renamed the Quantitative Research in the Life and Social Sciences Program (QRLSSP).

Castillo-Chavez was also the director of the Institute for Strengthening and the Joaquin Bustoz Math-Science Honors Program (JBMSHP), a summer residential mathematics program for students interested in academic careers requiring mathematics, science, or engineering-based coursework, particularly those from underrepresented groups.<ref>{{Cite web | title=JBMSHP Home {{!}} Simon A. Levin Mathematical, Computational and Modeling Sciences Center | url=https://jbmshp.asu.edu/ | access-date=2026-04-28 | website=jbmshp.asu.edu}}</ref>

== Research ==
Castillo-Chavez has co-authored over 560 publications and a dozen books, including textbooks, research [[monograph]]s, and edited volumes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=xYcl1kgAAAAJ&hl=en |website=scholar.google.com |access-date=16 February 2024}}</ref><ref name="researchgate">{{cite web |title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez |url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Carlos-Castillo-Chavez |website=ResearchGate |access-date=16 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230120175834/https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Carlos-Castillo-Chavez |archive-date=20 January 2023}}</ref> His research explores the intersection of the mathematical, natural, and social sciences,<ref name="researchgate"></ref> focusing on how dynamic social landscapes affect disease dispersal, evolution, and control, as well as the impact of environmental risk, social structures, and human behavior on disease dynamics, including addiction.

He and his collaborators have introduced mathematical models for the spread of scientific concepts, ideas, or media-driven information, such as the [[social contagion]] effect in recurrent [[mass shooting|mass killings]] and [[school shootings]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Towers |first1=S |last2=Gomez-Lievano |first2=A |last3=Khan |first3=M |last4=Mubayi |first4=A |last5=Castillo-Chavez |first5=C |title=Contagion in Mass Killings and School Shootings. |journal=PLOS ONE |date=2015 |volume=10 |issue=7 |article-number=e0117259 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0117259 |pmid=26135941|doi-access=free|pmc=4489652 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1017259T |hdl=2286/R.I.42220 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> They have also studied the role of behavior and mobility in the dynamics of emergent and re-emergent diseases, including [[Ebola]], [[influenza]], [[tuberculosis]], and [[Zika virus]]. His publications have also included models and frameworks for collaborative learning based on the activities of the ASU Mathematical and Theoretical Biology Institute.<ref>{{cite web |title=Director's Welcome |website=Simon A. Levin Mathematical, Computational and Modeling Sciences Center |publisher=Arizona State University |url=https://mcmsc.asu.edu/Directors-Welcome |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190221112451/https://mcmsc.asu.edu/Directors-Welcome |archive-date=21 February 2019}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
His awards and recognition include:
* Three White House Awards (1992, 1997, and 2011). His MTBI program received the Presidential Awards for Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentoring (PAESMEM).<ref>https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_images.jsp?cntn_id=122273&org=NSF 29 January, 2025</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Efforts in mentoring underrepresented groups in math and science are recognized at White House ceremony on Sept. 11 &#124; Cornell Chronicle | url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/1997/09/cornells-castillo-chavez-receives-presidential-honor }}</ref>
* The 12th American Mathematical Society Distinguished Public Service Award in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web| title=2010 Award for Distinguished Public Service | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/201004/rtx100400528p.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101203003652/http://www.ams.org/notices/201004/rtx100400528p.pdf | archive-date=2010-12-03}}</ref>
* The 2007 Mentor Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS).<ref>{{cite web | title=2007 Mentor Award Recipient &#124; American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) | url=https://www.aaas.org/awards/mentor/2007 }}</ref>
* The 17th recipient of the SIAM Prize for Distinguished Service to the Profession.<ref>{{cite web | title=SIAM Prize for Distinguished Service to the Profession &#124; SIAM | url=https://www.siam.org/Prizes-Recognition/Major-Prizes-Lectures/Detail/siam-prize-for-distinguished-service-to-the-profession#Prize-History }}</ref>
* Member of the Board of Higher Education at the National Academy of Sciences (2009-2015) and served on President Barack Obama's Committee on the National Medal of Science (2010-2015).<ref>{{cite web | title=The National Medal of Science - Office of the Director (OD) &#124; NSF - National Science Foundation | url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/carloscastillochavez.jsp }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez Appointed to President's Committee on the National Medal of Science &#124; NIMBioS | url=http://www.nimbios.org/wordpress/2013/04/02/carlos-castillo-chavez-appointed-to-presidents-committee-on-the-national-medal-of-scien/ }}</ref>
* Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science; Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics; Founding Fellow of the American Mathematical Society; and American College of Epidemiology.<ref>{{cite web | title=Carlos Castillo-Chavez &#124; SIAM | url=https://sinews.siam.org/About-the-Author/carlos-castillo-chavez }}</ref>
* Held honorary Professorships at Xi'an Jiatong University in China, the Universidad de Belgrano in Argentina, and East Tennessee State University. Past appointments include a Stanislaw M. Ulam Distinguished Scholar at Los Alamos National Laboratory, a Cátedra Patrimonial at UNAM in México, and a Martin Luther King Jr. Professorship at MIT.<ref>https://mlkscholars.mit.edu/ccchavez/</ref>
* On February 24, 2016, the University Francisco Gavidia inaugurated the Centro de Modelaje Matemático Carlos Castillo-Chavez in the City of San Salvador, El Salvador.<ref>{{cite web | title=Centro de Modelaje Matemático Carlos Castillo Chávez | url=http://icti.ufg.edu.sv/cmmc3.html#.XGzKZHd95Z1 }}</ref>
* Served on NSF's Advisory Committee for Education and Human Resources (2016-2019) and on NSF's Cyber Infrastructure Advisory Boards (2016-2019).<ref>{{cite web | title=Directorate for STEM Education (EDU) &#124; NSF - National Science Foundation | url=https://www.nsf.gov/ehr/advisory_members.jsp }}</ref>
* The inaugural recipient of the William Yslas Velez Outstanding STEM Award, co-sponsored by the Victoria Foundation and the Pasqua Yaqui Tribe of Arizona (2015).<ref>https://www.science.org/content/article/adventures-mathematical-biologist 12 December 2003</ref>
* Elected as a Member-at-Large of the Section on Mathematics of the AAAS (2016–2020).<ref>{{cite web | title=Mathematics (A) &#124; American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) | url=https://www.aaas.org/governance/section-a }}</ref>
* In April 2017, [[Brown University]] invited Castillo-Chavez to present a lecture in the Series "Thinking Out Loud," titled "The Role of Contagion in the Building and Sustainability of Communities."<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211210/y5wELo08J9w Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20190128014144/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y5wELo08J9w Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite AV media| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y5wELo08J9w| title = Carlos Castillo-Chavez {{!}} Thinking Out Loud | website=[[YouTube]]}}{{cbignore}}</ref>
* Pete C. Garcia, Victoria Foundation - Higher Education Award. Outstanding Latina/o Faculty: Research in Higher Education Award. September 4, 2019.
